summary: A best current practice describing how to delegate reverse DNS (IN-ADDR.ARPA) for address blocks smaller than 256 addresses, which do not fall on the usual octet boundaries. It uses a naming trick so the owner of a small block can run their own reverse zone.

eli5.summary: Reverse lookups were handed out in big chunks. This trick lets someone with only a few addresses get their own small piece of the address book.

questions: how to delegate in-addr.arpa for a small subnet
reverse dns for fewer than 256 addresses
how to delegate reverse dns for a small subnet
why use cname records in reverse dns
subtitle: How to hand a small block of addresses its own reverse DNS zone using CNAME records.

tldr.problem: Reverse DNS zones follow octet boundaries, so a block of fewer than 256 addresses cannot be delegated to its own owner. Only one organization can administer the shared zone.
tldr.mechanism: The parent zone keeps a CNAME for each address, pointing into a new child zone named after the block (for example 128/26). That child zone is delegated to the block's owner and holds the PTR records.
tldr.outcome: Small blocks can be assigned and still get their own IN-ADDR.ARPA authority, with no change to DNS lookup software. It is a Best Current Practice, BCP 20.

facts.label: Parent zone cost
facts.value: Close to 256 CNAME records per split chunk

today: RFC 2317 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 20), and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2317 describes a way to delegate IN-ADDR.ARPA (reverse DNS) on non-octet boundaries, for address spaces covering fewer than 256 addresses. This removes one objection to subnetting on non-octet boundaries. It also makes it possible to assign address space in chunks smaller than 24-bit prefixes without losing the ability to delegate authority for the matching reverse mappings.

The method is fully compatible with the original DNS lookup mechanisms in RFC 1034. The lookup algorithm does not change, and no software that does DNS lookups needs modification. The document also gives some operational guidance.
sections.eli5: It is a way to give even a tiny group of computers its own page in the Internet's reverse address book, without changing how anyone looks things up.

sections.title: Why Small Blocks Are a Problem
sections.content:
Classless routing made it feasible to assign address space on non-octet boundaries. Giving a very small organization a full 24-bit prefix (the traditional “class C”) often wastes address space. A longer prefix, though, seems to leave the organization unable to run its own reverse zone.

The RFC's example splits 192.0.2.0 between three parties: 192.0.2.0/25 to organization A, 192.0.2.128/26 to B and 192.0.2.192/26 to C. The classical approach puts all the PTR records in one zone, 2.0.192.in-addr.arpa. Authority for a zone can only be delegated once, which usually means one organization administers it, and the other two depend on that organization for their address-to-name translation.
sections.eli5: If three families share one page in the address book, only one of them can hold the pen. The other two have to ask that family every time they want a change.

sections.title: Delegating Through CNAME Records
sections.content:
Since a zone can only be delegated once, the method adds more delegation points by extending the IN-ADDR.ARPA tree downwards. A new child zone is named from the first address of the block, or the first address plus the mask length, for example 0/25, 128/26 and 192/26.

In the parent zone (2.0.192.in-addr.arpa), each block gets NS records for its child zone, and each individual address gets a CNAME that points into that child zone, such as 129 CNAME 129.128/26.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa.. The child zone, for example 128/26.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa, is run by the block's owner and holds the real PTR records.

For each size-256 chunk split this way, close to 256 CNAME records are needed in the parent zone. The RFC admits some people find this ugly, but notes the records are easy to generate automatically once the partitioning is known. A record can be abbreviated to 129 CNAME 129.128/26.

The advantage over other proposals is that no already-deployed software needs to change. The RFC also says the technique had been in use for several years in many installations, apparently with no ill effects.

The examples use “/” in the names because it is visible. Some DNS implementations dislike special characters, so the RFC advises not copying the examples exactly and using a more conservative character such as a hyphen. It points to RFC 2181 to show such names are legal, and says the host-name restriction in RFC 952 does not apply because these are not host names.
sections.eli5: On the shared page, each address gets a sticky note: 'for the answer, go to the Smiths' own book'. The Smiths then keep their own book, and lookups just follow the note.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The technique is meant for delegating fewer than 256 addresses. For larger blocks the traditional method of multiple delegations can be used instead.

Some older name server software does not go and find the pointed-to name in a CNAME when it is not already known locally, so only the CNAME comes back and resolvers can be confused. To avoid this, the RFC recommends that the authoritative servers for the delegating (parent) zone also run as slave (secondary) servers for the child zones the CNAMEs point into.

CNAME referrals cannot be done twice for the same address space. You cannot give a /25 to one organization using this method and then have it subnet that /25 and repeat the trick, because that would make a CNAME point to a CNAME, which may be less robust. The RFC also mentions that some old beta releases of BIND 4.9.3 had a bug with CNAMEs during reverse lookups, which had been resolved in released code.
sections.eli5: Make sure the keeper of the main page also keeps a copy of each family's little book, and do not point a note at another note, because that gets confusing.

sections.title: Alternative Naming Conventions
sections.content:
Because the CNAMEs can point anywhere, the child zone does not have to be under IN-ADDR.ARPA or named after the address block. The RFC shows CNAMEs such as 1 CNAME 1.A.domain. that point into an ordinary domain, where the PTR records live next to the forward A records. A separate set of secondaries for the reverse zone is then not needed.

This is also needed when two organizations share one physical subnet with no neat alignment of addresses but still want to run their own reverse mappings. Lookups still travel through the IN-ADDR.ARPA tree, so the CNAMEs there must point in the right direction.
sections.eli5: The note can point to any book at all, not just one named after the address, so a family can keep names and numbers together in one place.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: With this scheme a leaf site relies on one more site running its DNS service correctly than it would with a /24 allocation of its own. That adds a component that must work for reliable name resolution. Apart from that, the authors were not aware of any additional security issues introduced by the mechanism.
sections.eli5: The only catch is that your address-book entry now depends on one more person doing their job well.

viz.caption: PARENT ZONE EXCERPT FOR THE /26 AT 128 (FROM RFC 2317)

data.title: Parent zone 2.0.192.in-addr.arpa
data.code:
$ORIGIN 2.0.192.in-addr.arpa.
128/26          NS      ns.B.domain.
128/26          NS      some.other.name.server.too.
129             CNAME   129.128/26.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa.
130             CNAME   130.128/26.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa.

$ORIGIN 128/26.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa.
129             PTR     host1.B.domain.
130             PTR     host2.B.domain.
